text: Everything in this chapter has been building toward this: shipping a new version of a running application safely, and undoing it in seconds if it turns out to be broken. Both operations run through the same Deployment and ReplicaSet mechanism from Lesson 10 — this lesson just puts that mechanism to work for real, end to end, with kubectl.

kubectl set image updates the Deployment's container image with one command, no new YAML file and no deleting anything first. The Deployment controller creates a new ReplicaSet with that template and starts shifting replicas over. maxUnavailable zero and maxSurge one is the safest common setting — it guarantees capacity never drops below target, briefly going one Pod above target to make the swap possible.

kubectl rollout status blocks until the rollout finishes or fails, printing its progress as replicas update one at a time. That makes it a natural health gate inside a CI/CD pipeline step — if the new Pods never pass their readiness check, this command times out with a non-zero exit code instead of hanging silently forever.

Rollback is possible at all because Kubernetes never actually deletes an old ReplicaSet on update — it scales it to zero and keeps it around as a revision. kubectl rollout history lists those retained revisions by number, and undoing a Deployment means scaling a previous ReplicaSet back up while scaling the current one down.

kubectl rollout undo reverts to the immediately prior revision; adding to-revision targets any specific one further back. And the rollback itself is a rolling update — it respects the exact same maxSurge and maxUnavailable settings, so reverting a bad release is just as gradual and just as safe as the deploy that caused the problem.

Deploy, update, roll back — all through the same object hierarchy this chapter started with. Next chapter moves to networking: Services, Ingress, and how traffic actually reaches the Pods you can now manage with confidence.
